epics.title: Hive settings page
epics.description: A control-plane page in the hive repo at hive.sparktobloom.com/settings — the admin console plugged into the operational heart of the hive: mind lifecycle, voice, tooling, and cross-hive federation. Design system: reuse hive's existing layout.html and style.css chrome, tabbed content area, same as /graph, /memory and /rules. Daniel expects to keep adding requirements as this gets built — the source doc is living, not a frozen spec.
epics.requirements: Seven sections, each at its own stage: mind registry with per-mind configuration, hive-tools status, voice server configuration, new-mind creation, downloads, hive-to-hive federation, and a hive-comms placeholder.
epics.acceptance_criteria: Every section either works against live state or carries a clearly-labelled placeholder. Nothing on the page implies a capability it does not have.
epics.qa_tests: Per feature. The through-line: every card reads from live state — broker rows, container health, health checks — rather than from a config file someone has to keep current.

features.title: Voice server configuration
features.description: Mostly done. hive-mind-voice (chatterbox) and hive-mind-voice-kokoro are both health-checked live. Chatterbox voice cloning is confirmed: voice_server.py's _resolve_voice_ref reads minds/<name>/voice_ref.wav fresh on every request rather than caching at startup, so no new upload API was needed on the voice server itself — the settings page writes straight to that same path (hive_mind's minds/ directory, mounted read-write at /minds_hive_mind_voice, scoped separately from the read-only mount the mind registry uses) and it is live on the mind's next TTS call.
features.requirements: The one gap recorded at the time: no per-mind voice-server assignment, chatterbox versus kokoro, existed anywhere in config — confirmed by grepping every mind's runtime.yaml for VOICE_API_URL with nothing overriding it — so it read as global-server, per-mind-clip. That gap has since been closed: voice and voice_engine are now fields on the mind, travelling the path the model travels, with runtime.yaml as the truth and the broker row as the cache every speaking surface reads.
features.acceptance_criteria: Both voice servers health-check live, a clip upload is live on the next TTS call, and a mind's engine is a field on the mind rather than a URL in each caller's environment.
features.qa_tests: Uploading a clip changes the next reply's voice with no restart. A mind naming kokoro is spoken by kokoro and one naming chatterbox by chatterbox. A mind naming a clip that is not on the server is refused rather than spoken in the fallback — chatterbox caches the last reference it was handed, so a silent fallback is a reply in a voice nobody chose and nobody can notice.

epics.title: Agent-Native Memory System Design Review
epics.description:
A review of 'Are We Ready For An Agent-Native Memory System?' (arxiv 2606.24775, June 2026) against the hive's own memory stack. The authors treat agent memory as a standalone data management problem and decompose it into four modules — representation and storage, extraction, retrieval and routing, and maintenance. They ran systematic experiments across architectures and found no universal winner: graph-based memory wins at cross-session reasoning, hierarchical systems are better for long coherent dialogues, and trace-preserving approaches suit stateful execution. Their headline conclusion is that we are not yet ready for a universal agent-native memory system, with three critical gaps — temporal degradation (retrieval accuracy drops sharply when evidence and query are separated in time), update robustness (append-only stores produce hallucinations of the past because conflicts are never resolved), and long-horizon stability (memory coherence breaks down over extended sessions).

Where the hive stands today: the memory stack is a vector store (hive-lucent) for retrieval, an epilogue processor for extraction, and a knowledge graph for identity and soul. That maps onto the paper's four-module framework but has gaps in all three critical areas. Compression: the epilogue processor summarizes session content before storing it, which the paper identifies as the worst tradeoff, since raw evidence consistently outperforms summaries — we are doing exactly what they recommend against. Conflict resolution: if a mind learns something contradictory across two sessions, both versions are stored and whichever retrieves first wins; there is no versioning, no deduplication, and no semantic consolidation that flags or resolves conflicts. Retrieval: current retrieval is single-shot semantic search by embedding similarity, which the paper identifies as insufficient for exactly the temporal and cross-session queries a long-lived mind needs to answer well.
epics.requirements:
The paper's practical recommendations: preserve evidence fidelity over compression, because raw text outperforms summarized versions; use conservative consolidation rather than delayed flushing or coarse summarization; implement hybrid retrieval with explicit query planning rather than pure semantic search; do localized maintenance rather than global reorganization to control cost; and select architecture based on workload bottleneck rather than assumed universal superiority.

Three discrete improvements, in priority order: fidelity-preserving extraction, conflict detection on write, and a query planning layer.
epics.acceptance_criteria: Readiness assessment: the hive's memory is adequate for short-horizon use and single-session coherence. It will degrade over months as contradictory memories accumulate and compressed summaries replace the evidence needed for accurate retrieval. The paper's lightweight-system finding means this is not a crisis — but if the intent is for a mind to remain coherent over genuinely long-term engagement, the conflict resolution and fidelity fixes are worth doing before the store grows much larger. The query planning layer is the highest-leverage single change and the least disruptive to the existing architecture.
epics.qa_tests: The paper's own failure modes are the tests: retrieval accuracy against a query whose evidence is months old, a contradictory pair of memories resolving to the newer one rather than to whichever retrieves first, and coherence across an extended session. None of these are unit tests — they are judged by reading what the mind recalls.

features.title: Fidelity-preserving extraction
features.description: Priority one. Store raw or near-raw session excerpts alongside summaries rather than replacing them. The cost is storage; the benefit is retrieval quality over time. Lucent's vector store can hold both; the epilogue processor needs to emit both.
features.requirements: The epilogue processor emits raw excerpts alongside its summaries rather than instead of them.
features.acceptance_criteria: The evidence survives the summary.
features.qa_tests: A detail present in the raw session but absent from the summary is recallable afterwards. Today it is not, which is the whole finding.

stories.title: Emit raw excerpts alongside summaries
stories.description: The processor currently replaces the evidence with a summary. Keep both.
stories.requirements: Both stored, both retrievable.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A summarised-away detail is still findable.
stories.qa_tests: Seed a session with a specific detail the summariser drops, then query for it. Recall returns it from the raw excerpt.

features.title: Conflict detection on write
features.description: Priority two. When the epilogue processor stores a new memory, query for semantically similar existing memories and flag contradictions. A simple approach: retrieve the top three candidates, have the mind score them for contradiction, and mark conflicting entries as superseded rather than deleting them.
features.requirements: Contradiction detection at write time. Superseded rather than deleted, so the history survives.
features.acceptance_criteria: A contradicted memory does not win on retrieval order.
features.qa_tests: Write a fact, then write its contradiction. The newer one is returned and the older is marked superseded rather than returned alongside it or deleted outright. Note that scoring for contradiction is a mind's judgement, read rather than asserted — a regex or an assertion on it would be testing the wrong thing.

stories.title: Flag contradictions against the top candidates on write
stories.description: Retrieve the top three semantically similar memories, score for contradiction, mark the loser superseded.
stories.requirements: Marked superseded, never deleted.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The newer fact wins and the older is still inspectable.
stories.qa_tests: A contradictory pair resolves to the newer. The older is retrievable as superseded. The contradiction score is judged by reading the mind's reasoning, not asserted against a threshold.

features.title: Query planning layer
features.description: Priority three by the doc's ordering but named the highest-leverage single change and the least disruptive to the existing architecture. Before hitting the vector store, decompose the incoming context into a set of targeted sub-queries — temporal, factual, relational — and merge the results. A thin LLM call before retrieval that the paper shows significantly improves cross-session coherence.
features.requirements: Decomposition into temporal, factual and relational sub-queries, with merged results. One thin call ahead of retrieval.
features.acceptance_criteria: Cross-session coherence improves measurably against single-shot semantic search.
features.qa_tests: A query spanning two sessions and a time reference is answered correctly where single-shot search fails it. Measured as a comparison rather than asserted, since the improvement is in what comes back rather than in a return code.

stories.title: Decompose a query into temporal, factual and relational sub-queries
stories.description: A thin call ahead of retrieval, merging the results.
stories.requirements: Three query kinds, merged.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Cross-session and temporal queries improve.
stories.qa_tests: A set of queries that single-shot search answers badly is answered better. Judged by reading the recalled set against what the question needed.

epics.title: An information surface for the orchestration layer
epics.description:
A read surface on hive-comms that the skills an orchestrating mind runs can query mid-conversation, plus the harness-runs page widened from counts to records.

Why: a build orchestrator currently guesses at facts nobody has given it. Cypher's build-orchestrator skill is told to read a step-to-model mapping from build-models.json, a file that has never existed on this machine for any project, and is told in the same breath that she may never write it. Faced with that hole she invented model names — the literal string 'default', then 'gpt-4o-mini', then 'claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620' — and the proxy refused all three. Zero code was written. Nothing in the system recorded why. Two gaps, one cause: the orchestration layer has no live source of truth about itself.

Evidence: turn.completed for Cypher's dispatch on 2026-10-07 reported 28 tool calls emitted, 21 served, 7 failed, and nothing anywhere recorded what the 7 were. Her update_goal call that same morning was refused with 'goal_id must be non-empty' because she guessed the id instead of reading it; that refusal, too, exists only in a compressed transcript nobody would ever open.
epics.requirements:
The surface: a mind's skills can read the current step-to-model policy during a turn, without a credential the skill has to manage and without an endpoint open to anyone who can reach the host. A value changed while a conversation is running is visible to that conversation on its next read — nothing is handed over at spawn time and then held stale for the life of the session. The surface is read-only to agents; editing happens in the console. It lives on hive-comms, because every mind already points at comms, already holds a credential for it, and already has its session's model resolved by it, so remote minds reach it by construction — no new container, no new port per host, no new secret per install.

The model policy: keyed on pipeline step name — decompose, plan, story, review — not on mind and not on skill file, because those names are identical across minds given the orchestrator skill is the shared one, so one global table serves every mind. Each shipped build skill declares its own step name in frontmatter and the console page builds its rows from what the hive repo ships, so adding a step skill makes a row appear and nobody maintains a list. A step whose mapped model this mind's proxy key cannot address falls back to the mind's own model and says so in the run record — it does not fail the build and it does not silently substitute. A skill never invents a model name: with no name for a step it omits the model argument entirely, which runs the child on the mind's own model. build-models.json is deleted as a concept — no file in any repo, nothing to create, nothing to go stale.

The failure record: every tool call the harness could not serve is recorded at the moment it fails, durably, without anyone opening a transcript. The record distinguishes three cases, all of which the harness can tell apart by itself — a call whose name resolved to a real tool and returned an error (the model's fault, usually arguments); a call whose name resolved to no tool at all (a gap in our tooling); and a call the model never put on the wire, emitted as text in the reply channel instead. Whether a missing tool is one we should have is a verdict the operator sets on the page; the system never infers it. The escalation route reads this record, and only harness gaps escalate — a model fumbling its own arguments does not. An agent can read the known-gap list, so an orchestrator does not rediscover the same missing tool on every build.

Also on the surface, day one: the catalog of models this mind may actually address, so a skill picks from a real list rather than inventing one; and the roster of minds and what each is for.
epics.acceptance_criteria: An orchestrator reads its step-to-model policy rather than guessing it. A value edited in the console is visible to a running conversation on its next read. Every unserved tool call is recorded at the moment it fails, classified into one of the three cases. Only harness gaps escalate.
epics.qa_tests: The staleness property is the one to test deliberately: change a value mid-conversation and confirm the next read sees it, because a spawn-time handover that is then held for the life of the session is the failure this replaces. The three-way classification is testable because the harness can tell the cases apart by itself — a call that resolved to a real tool and errored, a call that resolved to no tool, and a call that never reached the wire.

features.title: The read surface on hive-comms
features.description: Where it lives and why. Every mind already points at comms, already holds a credential for it, and already has its session's model resolved by it; remote minds reach it by construction. No new container, no new port per host, no new secret per install. Deliberately not an MCP server: a tool table loaded at session start has the same staleness problem as spawn-time environment, plus a tool-table cost on every turn.

epics.title: Multi-user and authorization
epics.description:
Owner is the test bed for multi-user identity and group-based authorization, proven there and then carried to hive and every other personal site. The driver is concrete: Aiden writes recipes through Zack and wants them on owner's docs section, which today means Daniel pastes them by hand because owner has exactly one account and that account owns everything.

Current state: there is no single shared database, and there are two identity stores. auth-service (~/Storage/Dev/auth-service) is FastAPI plus sqlite on :8600, cookie domain .sparktobloom.com, one seeded account, with owner, property lens, btc and apps as thin clients that read the auth_session cookie, GET /verify, and redirect to login on failure — owner's client is src/auth_client.py, which caches verified sessions for 30 seconds. hive (~/Storage/Dev/hive/src/auth.py) has its own sqlite and its own users table, self-contained by design. Owner today is 11 pages and roughly 30 routes, all behind the same single account.
epics.requirements:
Three layers, in order of importance: users and groups with CRUD on both; authorization applied to pages and to actions, starting at read-only versus full CRUD and extensible to finer grants; and an enforcement mechanism so a newly added page falls under the paradigm automatically rather than by the author remembering to wire it.

Two decisions are already made. First, hive stays clonable and the authorization model travels rather than the service: hive is open source and meant to be cloned and stood up by other people, it already leans on hive-tools and an inference proxy, and making a running auth-service a hard prerequisite makes that worse — this is exactly the over-customization that keeps the 3D modelling work in owner rather than hive. So the shared thing is the model and its enforcement, not a network dependency: hive keeps a self-contained default identity store that ships in the clone, and Daniel's install points at auth-service instead, the same substitution pattern already used for model providers — one interface, several backings. That preserves the reason for the test bed: what gets proven in owner and carried to hive is the schema, the grant semantics and the test that enforces them, reusable as a library over a pluggable store rather than as a URL other people have to run.

Second, a grant attaches to a route path, and routes are made to match resources. Rather than choose between page-level and resource-level, owner's routes get restructured so the two are the same thing: every collection worth granting separately becomes its own path — docs/recipes, docs/specs, docs/system-configuration, backlog, models/<folder>. The URL path is the resource identifier and a grant is held against a path prefix. The site is already most of the way there: /models/{folder:path} is a catch-all resolved against the model tree and /docs already navigates folders under a docs root, so extending that shape to the remaining sections is the work — and it makes the site better independent of authorization, with addressable sections instead of monolithic pages. Enforcement then sits at the one place every page render and every API call already passes through: the resolver that turns a request path into content. Page-level authorization falls out as the degenerate case of a prefix with one thing under it.
epics.acceptance_criteria:
Aiden can write a recipe through Zack and have it land on owner's docs section without Daniel pasting it by hand. A page added after this lands guarded by default rather than by the author remembering.

A limit, stated rather than discovered later: a path prefix addresses a tree, not a row. The row-shaped collections — /api/spending/items, /api/btc/purchases — are one route over many rows with no path that separates one row from another, so those are granted whole-route, all rows or none, which is correct while they hold only Daniel's financial data. The first row-shaped collection two people must share differently is the point where a second mechanism becomes necessary.
epics.qa_tests: The enforcement test is the one that earns its keep: a newly added page is guarded without the author wiring anything, which is only testable by adding a page and checking it is refused to an unauthorized user. Two open questions have to be answered before implementation: is the grant model per-user, per-group, or both; and where does enforcement live so a new page cannot ship unguarded. Two risks to hold: per-row sharing inside a single collection has no answer in the path-prefix model, and two implementations of the same model (hive's built-in store and auth-service) can still drift — shared code narrows that, shared tests close it, and nothing yet forces either.

epics.title: Consolidated Telegram and Discord surface bots
epics.description:
One Telegram bot and one Discord bot, shared by every mind, so a feature landed once is a feature every mind has.

Why: there are three unrelated implementations today. hive-edge-minds carries the most complete pair — 1782 lines of Telegram and 697 of Discord, with streaming replies, the session picker, cross-surface pickup, rename, voice, image intake, queue draining and skill invocation — and Skippy and Mordecai both run it from the same remote, so those two stay in step by pulling. hive_mind/bots/ carries an older pair, about 890 lines of Telegram, which is what the containerised minds in the stack run: Ada, Bilby, Bob, Cypher, Nagatha. hermes carries its own, which Dragoman and mini-boss run, sharing no code with either of the above. A feature therefore has to be written up to three times, and in practice is written once and the other two drift. The typing indicator is the example that started this: Dragoman and mini-boss showed a live typing indicator while the edge pair showed a bare ellipsis until 2026-10-05.
epics.requirements: Decided: a shared core plus per-mind extensions, not strict parity — the conversation plumbing is identical everywhere, and a mind may still carry a command no other mind has, so Bilby's triage command does not become everyone's. The core is based on the hive-edge-minds pair, because it is the most complete and nothing in it is mind-specific: it talks to COMMS_URL and reads its own tokens from the environment, so a mind's identity never enters the bot. The core is a new public repo, hive-surfaces — public removes the credential problem entirely, with a plain pip install from a git URL, no deploy key, no build secret, no submodule recursion, and hermes consuming it as easily as the stack does; the bots carry no tokens, chat ids, addresses or personal content, so there is nothing to withhold. A mind extends the core by registering extra commands into it: the core owns the handler table and the process and a mind hands it additional commands — not a library a per-mind bot imports and wires itself, which would let each mind's entry point drift, the thing being fixed. Every mind tracks the same floating main: no pins, no per-instance version to carry, so a feature is live everywhere the moment it merges, which is the point of consolidating in the first place; the accepted cost is that a bad commit reaches every mind at once, which makes the core's own test suite a gate rather than an oracle. The core names no mind and no person — three things in the current code violated this and were generalized in the lift: two comments naming skippy.service, and the photo handler's instruction to file an image into 'the active house's images folder', which is Skippy's property workflow in generic code. Every mind runs the core, containerised minds included; for them this replaces hive_mind/bots/ and is a bot swap only.
epics.acceptance_criteria: Four sequenced steps, the first two done 2026-10-05. Not in scope: nothing about how a mind is deployed, hosted or registered changes, and no mind becomes a different kind of mind. This is a bot swap.
epics.qa_tests: The core's own suite is the gate, since main is what every surface in the hive is running — nothing merges there red. Per mind at switchover: enumerate that mind's current commands and confirm each one is either in the core or registered as that mind's own extension. A command that is neither is a parity hole, not an acceptable loss.

features.title: Create hive-surfaces
features.description: Done. Public at github.com/danielstewart77/hive-surfaces, 181 tests green. The lift generalized the three namings, moved the photo drop to a configured directory — a path derived from the module's location is inside site-packages once installed, which the next reinstall wipes — and added the two things the lift needed that the fork never had: configuration injected by the host, and a command registration seam. Three test files were not carried, because they read telegram_bot.py as text and asserted on substrings.
features.requirements: Public repo, no mind or person named, configuration injected by the host, a command registration seam.
features.acceptance_criteria: A plain pip install from a git URL works with no credential.
features.qa_tests: 181 tests green. The three dropped test files were reading source as text and asserting on substrings, which is exactly the shape that passes regardless of behaviour.

stories.title: Lift the edge pair into a public core
stories.description: Generalize the three namings, configure the photo directory, add host-injected configuration and a command registration seam.
stories.requirements: No mind-specific content; two new seams.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Public, installable, 181 tests green.
stories.qa_tests: Covered by the core's own suite. The host hands over a whole SurfaceConfig rather than keywords, because keywords alone change only the fields they name — a host that configured its allow-lists at boot and later names a model must not have that call blank the allow-list back to authorizing nobody.

Mordecai's image is rebuilt and the core is installed in his running container, so a recreate whenever Daniel picks the moment boots clean. Both minds keep their old in-memory bots until restarted.

features.acceptance_criteria: Both minds run the core after their next restart.
features.qa_tests: 673 tests green in the edge repo. Verified live by restarting and watching a turn complete on each surface.

features.title: hermes last
features.description: And only if Dragoman and mini-boss keep that codebase. It is the only consumer outside both existing implementations, so it is the one that proves whether the extension seam is real rather than a shape that happens to fit code it was extracted from.

features.qa_tests: This is the real test of the extension seam. A seam that only fits the code it came from is not a seam, and hermes is the only consumer that can show the difference.
